text.text: Cognitive Distortions are unhelpful thinking patterns that Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) aims to identify and restructure, so classifying cognitive distortions is a crucial process for reframing.
The classification becomes difficult as the data is limited, and the data are imbalanced most of the time.
We study dominant distortion classification on the publicly available Therapist Q&A dataset (Shreevastava and Foltz, 2021) where the annotator agreement on the dominant distortion is low (34%).
text.formatted: We study dominant distortion classification on the publicly available Therapist Q&A dataset (Shreevastava and Foltz, 2021) where the annotator agreement on the dominant distortion is low (34%).

text.text: Using the annotated distorted span as input, we compare TF-IDF baselines with RoBERTa, DeBERTa-v3 and MentalBERT (with and without focal loss) over three seeds, reporting accuracy, macro F1 and Cohen's kappa with significance tests.

The encoders reach 0.39 to 0.44 accuracy, well above the majority-class baseline (0.15), the three crossentropy encoders are not significantly different from each other, while the weighted focal loss is worse.

An error analysis shows that errors concentrate on a small group of overlapping distortions, mainly All-or-nothing thinking, Magnification and Mental filter, which suggests that unclear category boundaries limit performance more than model choice.
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is a widely used treatment for people who struggle with negative thought patterns, which are common in depression and anxiety (Hofmann et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is a widely used treatment for people who struggle with negative thought patterns, which are common in depression and anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Hofmann et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The central goal of the CBT is to identify these patterns known as cognitive distortion, and to help the person reframe them (Beck, 1963).
text.formatted: The central goal of the CBT is to identify these patterns known as cognitive distortion, and to help the person reframe them <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Beck, 1963)</ref>.

text.text: As digital and online therapy become more accessible, the need for automated tools that recognize distortion in text is growing.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) offers a practical route to this with suitable data and models; a system could flag a distortion in what a person writes and support reframing between therapy sessions.
Such a tool would assist therapists and users, not replace them.
Classifying distortion is difficult for several reasons; labelled data is rarely available, and classes are imbalanced.
The categories also overlap and trained annotators often disagree.
On the Therapist Q&A Dataset, agreement on the dominant distortion is only 34% (Shreevastava and Foltz, 2021).
text.formatted: On the Therapist Q&A Dataset, agreement on the dominant distortion is only 34% <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Shreevastava and Foltz, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Later work on this dataset studied a multi-step pipeline (Phan et al., 2025) that first extracts the distorted span and then classifies it.
text.formatted: Later work on this dataset studied a multi-step pipeline <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Phan et al., 2025)</ref> that first extracts the distorted span and then classifies it.

text.text: However, a controlled comparison of model families that reports variation across random seeds, statistical tests, and an error analysis is still missing.
Rather than focusing only on classification performance, we examine which distortions are confused, using the average confusion pattern of the four encoders and per-class scores across all models.
These patterns can reveal the limitations in the current dataset and classification formulation, and offer useful insights for developing more reliable cognitive distortion detection systems.
In this paper, we study dominant distortion classification over 10 classes, using the annotated distorted span as input.
We compare TF-IDF baselines with three transformer encoders under identical settings and three seeds; we report accuracy, macro F1 and Cohen's kappa with significance tests.
Our contributions are: A controlled comparison of six models on dominant distortion classification, with results averaged over three seeds.
Evidence that three cross-entropy encoders do not differ significantly from each other, although they tend to outperform the TF-IDF baselines.
An error analysis showing that mistakes concentrate on small groups of overlapping distortions, which suggests that unclear category boundaries limit performance more than model choice.

Cognitive distortion detection has grown quickly, but a recent survey of 38 studies described the field as fragmented, with inconsistent taxonomies, task formulations and evaluation practices, and few shared benchmarks (Sage et al., 2025).

text.text: Other work addresses the imbalance that we also face. Ding et al. (2022) compared data augmentation with domain specific MentalBERT on rare distortions in therapy messages, and found the domain-specific model gave larger gains than augmentation.

text.text: Our study differs in scope: we compare model families under identical conditions on one fixed task, report variation across seeds with significance tests, and analyze which distortions are confused.
Limited data is a common obstacle in mental health NLP, because the conversations are confidential and rarely shared.
We use the Therapist Q&A Dataset (Shreevastava and Foltz, 2021), which contains anonymized patient questions collected from Kaggle.
text.formatted: We use the Therapist Q&A Dataset <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Shreevastava and Foltz, 2021)</ref>, which contains anonymized patient questions collected from Kaggle.

text.text: Each entry is a short message in which the patients share their situation, followed by a response from the therapist.

Annotators labeled each message with a dominant distortion, and a secondary distortion where one applied, chosen from 10 types; All or Nothing, Overgeneralization, Labeling, Fortune telling, Mind reading, Emotional Reasoning, Should Statements, Magnification, Mental filter and personalization.
They also marked the part of the messages where the distortion appears, which we call a distorted span.
For the dominant distortion, the original author reports a joint probability of agreement of 33.7% between two annotators, measured on about 730 messages.
In our study, we drop the messages labeled "No Distortion" and keep the 1,597 distorted messages, using only dominant labels.
We hold a stratified test set of 240 messages and use the remaining 1,357 for the training and validation.
All models use the same split.

Following earlier work that found distorted spans more informative than full message (Varadarajan et al., 2025; Phan et al., 2025), we predict the dominant distortion from the annotated distorted span.
text.formatted: Following earlier work that found distorted spans more informative than full message <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Varadarajan et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Phan et al., 2025)</ref>, we predict the dominant distortion from the annotated distorted span.

text.text: The split is fixed for all models: a stratified test set of 240 messages (split seed 3407) and 1,357 messages for training and validation.
We use TF-IDF features with Logistic Regression and random forest.
The regularization strength and the tree depth are chosen by 5-fold cross validation on the training data, using macro F1.

We fine-tune three pretrained encoders for sequence classification: RoBERTa-base, DeBERTa-v3-base and MentalBERT, a BERT model pretrained on mental health text that Ding et al. (2022) also used for distortion classification.
text.formatted: We fine-tune three pretrained encoders for sequence classification: RoBERTa-base, DeBERTa-v3-base and MentalBERT, a BERT model pretrained on mental health text that <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Ding et al. (2022)</ref> also used for distortion classification.

text.text: MentalBERT is trained with two losses, standard cross-entropy and a weighted focal loss (gamma = 2, class weights proportional to inverse class frequency).
Because the focal variant also uses class weights, any difference from cross-entropy mixes the two effects.
For encoders, we ran 5-fold cross-validation (6 epochs, learning rate 3e-5, batch size 16) to check that this configuration was stable (Table 1).
text.formatted: For encoders, we ran 5-fold cross-validation (6 epochs, learning rate 3e-5, batch size 16) to check that this configuration was stable (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Crossvalidation accuracy was within about one point of test accuracy, RoBERTa and MentalBERT (CE) were tied in both, and DeBERTa-v3 was lowest.
We then fixed this configuration for all encoders.
Crossvalidation chose C = 30 for logistic regression in all seeds and a tree depth of 60, 60 and unlimited for random forest.
We train for up to 10 epochs (15 for DeBERTa-v3, which converged more slowly in our trials).
We keep 10% of the training data for early stopping in macro F1 (patience 3) and evaluate the best checkpoint once in the test set.
Every model is run with three training seeds (1,2 and 3) separate from the split seed.
We report mean and standard deviation of accuracy, macro-F1, weighted F1, and Cohen's kappa against the gold labels.
A majorityclass predictor serves as reference.
To compare models, we ran McNemar test on each seeds predictions and report the p-value for each seed.
Because the three seeds use the same test set, the per seed pvalues are not independent, so we do not combine them.
We also computed a paired bootstrap (5,000 resamples of the test messages) on the accuracy difference averaged over seeds, and call a difference significant only if its 95% interval excludes zero.
Table 2: Test results for each model (mean ± standard deviation over three seeds).
Majority class baseline reaches 0.15 accuracy.
Table 3: Pairwise comparison between the top models: accuracy difference, 95% paired bootstrap interval, exact McNemar p-values for seeds 1, 2 and 3.
The differences between the three cross-entropy encoders are not statistically significant (Table 3), so none of them is reliably better than the others.
text.formatted: The differences between the three cross-entropy encoders are not statistically significant (Table <ref type="table">3</ref>), so none of them is reliably better than the others.

text.text: Weighted focal loss is worse than MentalBERT (CE) by 5.0 points.
RoBERTa and MentalBERT (CE) beat TF-IDF + LR by about 7 points, and their bootstrap intervals exclude 0.
The McNemar p-values are 0.008 and 0.005 in seed 2, but the differences are not significant in the other two seeds, so the evidence is suggestive but not conclusive.
For MentalBERT (focal) and DeBERTa-v3, the interval includes 0, so their advantage over TF-IDF + LR is not significant.

The per-class results (Table 4) show that Allor-nothing thinking, mental filter and emotional reasoning were consistently weak, falling between 0.1 and 0.3, while mind reading, labeling, and fortune telling were easy to identify, falling between 0.5 and 0.6, with mind reading at 0.65.
text.formatted: The per-class results (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">4</ref>) show that Allor-nothing thinking, mental filter and emotional reasoning were consistently weak, falling between 0.1 and 0.3, while mind reading, labeling, and fortune telling were easy to identify, falling between 0.5 and 0.6, with mind reading at 0.65.

text.text: The three cross-entropy encoders are within about three points of each other (0.415 to 0.442 accuracy), and none of the pairwise differences is significant.
MentalBERT (CE) has the highest mean, but its lead is smaller than the variation across seeds and the standard error of a 240-message test set.
Weighted focal loss was worse than crossentropy (0.392 vs 0.442 accuracy) and less stable (SD 0.046).
Because this variant uses class weights, we cannot tell whether the focal term or the weights caused the drop.
It raised the All-or-nothing F1 score (0.271 vs 0.207), but this is a single small class and probably noise.

MentalBERT (CE) and RoBERTa beat TF-IDF with logistic regression with kappa of about 0.37 vs 0.28, yet this advantage is significant under McNemar in only one of three seeds, because the p-values are 0.008 and 0.005.
Overall, scores of about 0.44 on ten classes are far above the majority baseline but still modest.
Errors are not spread evenly.
All-or-nothing thinking, mental filter and emotional reasoning have lowest F1, while mind reading, labeling and fortune telling are easier.

The confusion matrix (Figure 1), averaged over the four encoder models, shows a cluster of mutually confused classes (Table 5): 23% of All-ornothing thinking are predicted as mental filter and 16% as magnification and overgeneralization.
text.formatted: The confusion matrix (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>), averaged over the four encoder models, shows a cluster of mutually confused classes (Table <ref type="table">5</ref>): 23% of All-ornothing thinking are predicted as mental filter and 16% as magnification and overgeneralization.

text.text: Mental filter is the weakest class, with only 18% of its messages predicted correctly; 26% of messages are predicted as magnification and 25% as overgeneralization. 18% of magnification messages are predicted as overgeneralization.
Emotional reasoning is most often confused with fortune-telling 21% and magnification 14%.
The encoders show similar patterns: their off-diagonal confusion correlate at r = 0.70 to 0.80, and 6 to 8 of their 10 most frequent confusions are shared, so we show the average.

These distortions all involve a negative interpretation of the situation, such as focusing on the negative, exaggerating it so their definitions overlap (Shreevastava and Foltz, 2021; Sage et al., 2025), and the dataset authors report the same difficulty.

text.text: Our accuracy (0.44) is above the reported 34% agreement between annotators.

This does not mean the models beat human annotators, because the agreement figure was measured between two annotators before disagreements were resolved by discussion, while gold labels are resolved ones.
It does show that the 34% figure is not a hard ceiling on accuracy.
We compared TF-IDF baselines and three transformer encoders on dominant cognitive distortion classification, using the annotated distorted span and three seeds.

The encoders reach 0.39 to 0.44 accuracy and clearly outperform the majority class baseline, but the three cross-entropy encoders are not significantly different from each other, while the MentalBERT (Focal) is worse and their ad-vantage over TF-IDF with logistic regression is borderline.

Errors concentrate on small groups of overlapping distortions, mainly all-or-nothing, magnification and mental filter, which suggests that unclear category boundaries and noisy labels limit performance more than the choice of model.
Future work should revisit the category definitions, model multiple distortions per message, and evaluate on larger, independent data with clinical review.
All results come from one dataset, and the test set has 240 messages, 15-36 per class.
Differences of few points and per class F1 values are therefore uncertain, and the error analysis is exploratory.
With only three seeds, the estimation of variation is rough.
Annotator agreement is low, and a message may contain several distortions, yet we predict one dominant label, so some errors may be valid alternative labels.
We used human-annotated distorted spans as input, so we do not test a full automatic pipeline that must first find the span.
We did not correct for multiple comparisons across the model pairs.
Fine-tuning on 1,357 messages is noisy, and results can shift between full reruns.
The encoders share the same hyperparameters, with only the epoch limit changed for DeBERTa-v3 per model; tuning could change the ranking.
We did not include large language models in the comparison.
Finally, the data are public forum posts, and no clinician reviewed the predictions, so the results are not clinically validated.
This study uses a publicly available Therapist Q&A dataset (Shreevastava and Foltz, 2021) which contains publicly shared, annotated questions and responses.

text.text: The main aim of the research is to study the patterns in how cognitive distortion is classified and not intended to replace the therapist.

Since the labels are subjective and model accuracy is limited, we acknowledge all the ethical considerations and recommend that any use of cognitive distortion classification takes place in professional settings with clinical guidance and careful validation.
